Induction of AJT in Defence 
*221. SHRI S. AGNIRAJ: Will the Minister of DEFENCE be pleased to 
State: 
(a) what steps are being taken to induct AJT in Indian Air Force; 
(b) what is the reason for delay; 
(c) when it is likely to be inducted; and 
(d) whether financial constraints are prohibiting the implementation if so, 
the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES): to (c) 
Various options for acquisition of an Advanced Jet Trainer are per 
examination by the Government. It would not be possible to lay  a time 
limit for such a major procurement project. However, the ornament is 
keen on early finalisation of the issue. 
(d) No, Sir. 
SHRI S. AGNIRAJ: Madam, we have been carrying out research work 
on this for the past twenty years. Hundreds of pilots die every year. There is no 
proper guidance for the pilots. The hon. Minister says that no date or years has 
been fixed to induct AJT in the Indian Air Force. I would like to know from the 
hon. Minister whether he would give the exact year by which we can induct this 
aircraft in our force. 
SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES: Madam, this is a process that is going 
on for some decades. It began in 1982. There were ups and downs and there was 
an evaluation of aircraft and rejection of it. And, finally, the price negotiations 
have also taken a lot of time. We, now, have a report 

RAJYA  SABHA [4 December 2002 ] 
where the price negotiations have been completed and we are exaiming 
finally, these papers to prepare a Note for the Cabinet Committion 
Security and have this matter resolved once and for all. 
SHRI S. AGNIRAJ: Is any proposal to manufacture the traning aircraft 
in HAL or in any other company in the country? I would like to know from the 
hon. Minister whether any such proposal is pending before the Government. 
SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES: The HAL has produced an 
intermediate jet trainer and it is a matter of time before it gets inducted into 
the force. We are flying it in the Aero India in February, 2003.

Jai Prakash Rozgar Guarantee Yojana 
*223.   SHRI K. NATWAR SINGH: 
DR.T. SUBBARAMI REDDY:† 
WILL the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT pe pleased to state: 
 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Dr. T. Subbarami Reddy. 
2 

[4 December, 2002] RAJYA  SABHA 
(a) whether a Rs. 5,000 crore employment guarantee scheme known as Jai 
Prakash Rozgar Guarantee Yojana, in 130 most-backward districts of the country, 
will be launched this year; 
(b) if so, the details of the scheme; 
(c) whether a task force was set up by Government for selection of the 
districts to be included in the said scheme; 
(d) if so, what are the names of the districts selected; and 
(e) by when the work on this scheme is likely to be started? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI SHANTA 
KUMAR): (a) to (e) The Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
In his Budget Speech 2002-03 the Finance Minister announced to launch 
the Jai Prakash Rozgar Gu arantee Yojana (JPRGY) to provide employment 
guarantee to the unemployed in the most distressed districts of the country. A 
Task Force was set up under the chairm anship of the Minister of Rural 
Development, to design and implement the programme for employment 
generation in the districts. The Task Force had submitted its report. On the basis 
of the report of the Task Force the scheme is being formulated in consultation 
with the other concerned Ministries/ Departments. 
DR.T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: Madam, on 19th October, 2002, the hon. 
Minister had announced that they were going to have a new scheme, namely, the 
Jai Prakash Rozgar Guarantee Yojana; and, they were going to have Rs. 5,000 
crores every year during the Five Year Plan. Are they going to implement this 
scheme directly in all the 141 districts, as mentioned by him, recently? Will they 
ask the States to identify the dist ricts where the scheme has to be 
implemented? He had assured that his scheme would be implemented with in 
two months' time. Now, we are already in the first week of December. So, I 
would like to know from the hon. Minister whether he is in a position to start 
the scheme, now. 
Secondly, the hon. Minister if trying to get 1800 million dollars from the 
ADB and the World Bank for the purpose of connecting all the villages by roads. 
So, I would like to know whether he Is proposing to link this scheme with the 
Jai Prakash Rozgar Guarantee Yojana so that more employment opportunities 
could be created for the poor people.

Statement 
(a) and (b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) The CBI team during its visit to Lisbon held discussions with

SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Madam, it appears that

SHRI CHENNAMANENI VIDYA SAGAR RAO: Madam, it is not true to 
say that the CBI returned without any results. A series of meetings, on this 
matter, have taken place in the Ministry of External Affairs and also in the 
Ministry of Home Affairs. After the deliberations, it has been decided to make a 
formal request of extradition, as per the requirements of the Portugal law.The 
Government of India is determined to get back Abu Salem. So, this decision 
has been taken. 
SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Madam, since we have no 
Extradition Treaty with Portugal, what exactly is the action proposed to be taken

8 

[4 December, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER, IN CHARGE OF THE MINISTRY OF 
HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI L.K. ADVANI): Madam, the hon. Member is right that 
we do not have any Extradition Treaty w ith Portugal. Therefore, immediately 
after it was informed on 19th September that Abu Salem has been arrested in 
Lisbon, — he was on our wanted list — the Minister of External Affairs wrote a 
formal letter to the Portugal Government requesting that he be extradited to India, 
because a number of cases relating to serious offences are pending against him 
in Indian courts. Subsequently, the CBI team went there.The Embassy in Lisbon 
provided full assistance to our team.The CBI team had had elaborate discussions 
with Portuguese authorities.The Portuguese authorities were, all along, helpful. At 
no point of time, did we come across any difficulty, but they said that we have 
to proceed as per law. And, as per law, a formal extradition request has to come 
from the Government of India on the cases pending against him, with the 
requisite FIRs, evidences, etc.These are required to be furnished. Furthermore, 
under the Portuguese law, there is not provision of capital punishment. And, 
they do not extradite a person who can be given capital punishment in another 
country. So, they would like to have an assurance from the Government of India 
that even after being extradited, he would not be subjected to capital 
punishment. It will require the State Governments to give all the necessary 
evidence and get it translated in Portuguese. All this process takes its own 
time. They have assured us that, at the moment, he is being tried or he is being 
investigated in relation to offences committed there in Portugal under the 
violation of the law of immigration and so many other laws. They have said 
that 'you may rest assured that we are not going to release him, and, in the 
meanwhile, you complete your process.' They have taken a remand of 90 days. So, 
within those 90 days, the process required from the Government of India would 
be completed. And, we are hopeful that Abu Salem would be extradited to India.

SHRI L.K. ADVANI: Madam, our experience is that in all cases, on the

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES 
(SHRI BASANGOUDA R. PATIL): (a) to  (d) A statement is laid on the 
Table of House. 
Statement 
(a) Till the end of the IX Plan, the Government of India had been 
implementing a Group Insurance Scheme and a New Insurance Scheme for 
Handloom Weavers in the country including the State of Andhra Pradesh. The State 
Government of Andhra Pradesh had a availed itself of Central assistance under 
the Group Insurance Scheme. Howeve r, the State Government had not 
implemented the New Insurance Scheme during the years 2000-01 and 2001-02. 
(b)The information on district-wise number of weavers covered under the 
Group Insurance Scheme during the year 2001-02 is given in the Statement 
(See below). 
(c) and (d) Under the Group Insurance Scheme, the insurance cover per 
weaver was of Rs. 10,000/- for an annu al premium was shared equally by the 
beneficiary, the State Government and the Central Government. The scheme 
covered natural death of the weaver and was implemented in collaboration with 
the Life Insurance Corporation of India. The New Insurance Scheme 
implemented through United India Insurance Co. Ltd. (UIIC) provided a 
coverage of Rs. 1.00 lakh in the event of death or loss of two limbs or two eyes 
or permanent disability due to accident. It also provided for a coverage of Rs. 
50,000/- for loss of one limb or one eye. Under the scheme, insurance coverage 
was available in respect of damage of dwelling unit and raw materials also. The 
premium was Rs. 120/- per annum, with a contribution of Rs. 20/- by the weaver, 
Rs. 40/- by the State Government and Rs. 60/- by the Government of India. 
In accordance with the announcemen t made by the Hon'ble Prime 
Minister in his Independence Day address to the Nation on the 15th August, 2002, a 
special contributory insurance scheme for weavers and artisans combining the 
Janshree Bima Yojana administered by the Life Insurance Corporation with the 
Group Insurance Scheme has been included as a component in a 
comprehensive Weavers' Welfare Scheme, for

Planning Commission as per the prescribed procedure for appraisal.

Terrorist activities from Bhutan 
*222.  SHRI SURESH KALMADI: 
SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: 
Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the fact that the militants are 
carrying on terrorist activities on a large scale from Bhutan alongwith the 
Assam-Bhutan border; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the steps taken/proposed to be taken in 
this regard? 
(c) whether the Central Government have received any request from the 
State Government of Assam to flush out National Democratic Font for Bodoland 
(N.D.F.B.) militants; if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) Government's reaction thereto and steps contemplated in this 
direction? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY FOR HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I.D. SWAMI) :(a) to (d) The Government is aware about the existence of 
camps of Indian insurgent groups including National Democratic Front of 
Bodoland (NDFB) in Bhutan territory, which are being used by them for safe 
havens, sanctuary, training purposes and launching of operations against 
Indian civilians and security forces. The Government of Assam have also 
drawn the attention of the Central Government in this regard.

Bhutan territory has been taken up from time to time with the Royal 
Government of Bhutan (RGOB). The issue was also discussed in detail during 
the visits of External Affairs Minister of Bhutan from August 4 to 6, 2002 and 
Foreign Secretary from October 28 to 30, 2002, with the Bhutanese 
leadership. The RGOB have assured that they will not allow these elements to 
use their territory for activities prejudicial to the interests of India.

MINES (SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD): (a) The State Government of

notification dated 7.5.1992 prohibited mining operation without obtaining prior

District have been granted by, the State Government of Haryana subject to the

environmental clearance from the designated authority. The mining leases for 
major minerals (leases more than 5ha.) for rest of areas have been granted by the

50 

[4 December, 2002] RAJYA  SABHA 
the area of Point 3260, which is 1800 metre East of Loonda post. The 
intrusion was evicted by appropriate action of ground troops and Air Force on 2nd

occupation by our own troops. Being in close proximity of the Line of Control 
and the area not being physically occupied, Pakistan troops had intruded into this

observed presence of some Pakistan troops in the area of Point 3260 on 26th 
July 2002, and suitable action was taken to evict the intrusion and to restore the 
sanctity of the Line of Control. As such, no enquiry was ordered into the 
incident.

Pakistan intrusion in Kargil.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I.D. SWAMI): (a) On 6.8.2002 at around 9.10 a.m., information was 
received in police Station Saleha distt. Panna through Ramadhar Chaurasia that a 
person called Mallu Sen, aged between 70-75 years of village Patna Tamoli died 
and his wife Smt. Kuttu Bai intended to commit sucide on the funeral pyre of her

one Constable reached the village with arms. Around 1000 people had already 
gathered near the cremation ground. The funeral pyre of Mallu Sen was burning 
at one end and Smt. Kuttu Bai stood near the funderal pyre. The people who 
gathered at the spot were provoking Smt. Kuttu Bai to sit on the funeral pyre of 
her husband. Station Officer tried to dissuade them from doing this. But they 
paid no heed to him and pelted stones at the Station Officer. Then they 
forcibly made Smt. Kuttu Bai sit on her husband's funeral pyre. Station Officer 
caught hold of Smt. Kuttu Bai's hand and tried to pull her out of the funerl

but also assulted him. In the assault both the Station Officer and the constable 
sustained injuries. Smt. Kuttu Bai was forcibly made to sit on the funeral pyre

[4 December, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA

alongwith details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I. D. SWAMI): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) In June 2002, Pune Police seized fake judicial and nonjudicial 
stamp papers with a face value of more than Rs. 2,028 crore in a series of raids in 
Pune, Mumbai and Thane. Other materials, such as fake court stamps, fake 
revenue stamps, fake share transfer stamps, fake insurance stamps, printing 
machinery, stationery, computers, cash and a car were also recovered. A case has

arrested. In the second case, Delhi Police seized on May 7,2002 fake non-judicial 
stamp papers with a face value of Rs. six lakhs besides fake Indian Nepalese and US 
currencies in different stages of 'manufacture'. Five perosns were arrested. In another 
case of recovery of fake stamps papers, Chandigarh Police intercepted on July 
28, 2002, a Tata Safari vehicle with fake share transfer stamps, insurance 
stamps, postage stamps, revenue stamps, etc. of the face value of more than 
Rs. 2.30 crores. Four persons were apprehended in this case. A criminal case No. 
549/2000 was registered on 19.08,2002 in PS Uppar Pet, Bangalore city 
following exposure of criculation of fake stamp papers in Karnataka.The 
Gvoernment of Karnataka has intimated that a special investigation team headed 
by a senior police officer of the rank of Additional Director General of Police has 
already been constituted to investigate the case. The Government of 
Maharashtra has reported that various measures have been taken to address the 
problem. These include alerting the field officers about the use of counterfeit 
stamps, issuing general instructions regarding features for identifying 
counterfeit stamps, circulating list of suspicious stamp vendors to the Sub-
Registrar Offices and undertaking thorough and details scrutiny of the 
documents registered in the last two years.

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI

Renovation of Indraprastha Power Plant in Delhi 
1607.   SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is proposed to give a face-lift and revamp the Indraprastha 
Power Plant in the Capital; if so, the details of the renovation;

other agency; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (c) Indraprastha Power Generation 
Company Ltd. (IPGCL) has planned to carry out the Renovation & 
Modernization (R&M) work in all the four units of Indraprastha Power Plant (3 x 
62.5 MW +1 x 60 MW). The job of comprehensive study of R&M for the 
station has been entrusted to National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC). 
The cost of R&M as envisaged by NTPC will be around Rs. 1.5 crores to Rs. 2.0 
crores per MW for which a provison has been made in the Plan funds of the 
IPGCL. At present the station is operating at an average PLF of about 40% for 
the last 4 years. The maximum available out put of all the four units is ranging 
from 45 MW to 50 MW. After R&M, the station will operate at the installed 
name plate capacity of 247.5 MW with life extension of 10-15 years. The work 
is expected to be completed within 5 years.

Statement 
Details of the Power Sector Reform Fund 
As a part of measures to refo rm the power sector, the Committee 
recommended that State Government should consolidate the past liabilities and 
finance them through agreements for write-downs and future sector surpluses. 
However, going by the track record of State Governments, a mere statement of 
intent is unlikely to carry any weight from the other stakeholders, specifically 
existing creditors and prospective lenders. In order to enhance the credibility and 
mitigate the risk of policy reversals it is necessary to ring-fence both the 
liabilities and the inflows earmarked for the sector restructuring. In order to do 
this, the State Government should establish a Power Sector Reform Fund 
(PSRF). All existing liabilities of the sector should be transferred to the PSRF. 
The responsibility for servicing these liabilities, however, remains with the 
State Government and as noted later, these can be re-financed on better terms 
with Central Government support. Conc omitantly, existing receivables (the 
privatized utility can be contracted to recover them the on an incentive-sharing 
basis), privatisation proceeds, and gran ts from the Government of India and 
other donor agencies should be transferred to the PSRF to defray these 
liabilities. In addition, it wo uld receive a portion of the surplus from future 
operations as revenues, say, in the form of a PSRF surcharge, The PSRF 
would be drawn Upon in a pre-specified order of priority to meet the State 
Government's obligations in discharging its liabilities.

Rejection of Delhi Declaration at the climate change meet 
by the EU 
1618. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA: Will the Minister 
of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that European Union has rejected the draft of the 
Delhi Declaration circulated by the Indian Government at the climate change 
meet; 
(b) if so, what are the details of the draft circulated; and 
(c) what are the reasons given by the European Union for rejecting it? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (c) The European Union did not 
reject the draft of the Delhi Declaration. A group of developed countries, 
including the European Union wanted to initiate a process for beginning a 
dialogue on broader participation of countries in greenhouse gas mitigation 
commitments for period beyond 2012. This  was resisted successfully by the 
developing countries, including India, on the grounds that the per capita 
greenhouse gas emissions of the developing countries, in general, were low in 
comparison to the developed countries, and that the overriding priority for the 
developing countries was poverty eradication for which economic growth was 
essential. The Delhi Ministerial Declaration on Climate Change and Sustainable 
Development was adopted by all Parties as a consensus document.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ANNASAHEB M.K. PATIL): (a) to (e) Drinking 
water supply being a State subject, schemes for providing drinking water 
facilities are implemented by the State Governments from their own 
resources.The Government of India supp lements the efforts of the States by

Programme (ARWSP).The powers to plan, sanction and implement Rural Water

Annexure showing release and expenditure under Accelerated Rural Water 
Supply Programme including activities taken under DPP for the  
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
156 

[4 December, 2002] RAJYA   SABHA 
last five years, State-wise, is enclosed [See Appendix 197 Annexure No. 14]. 
Annexure showing expenditure under State Sector programme for Rural Water 
Supply during the last five years is enclosed. [See Appendix 197 Annexure No. 
15] 
The following noms and criteria are being adopted under Accelerated Rural 
Water Supply Programme for providing drinking water to rural population in 
the habitations: 
(a) 40 liters per capita per day (Ipcd) of safe drinking water for human 
beings. 
(b) 30 Ipcd additional for cattle in the Desert Development Programme 
Areas. 
(c) One hand-pump or stand post for every 250 persons. 
(d) The water source should exist within the habitation/within 1.6 km in the 
plains and within 100 mtrs. elevation in the hilly areas. 
[Water is defined as safe if it is free from biological contamination 
(guinea worms, cholera, typhoid etc.) and chemical contamination (excess fluoride, 
brackishness, iron, arsenic, nitrates)] 
Recently Government of India have approved the relaxations in the rural 
water supply norms in the following manner: - 
(a) The norms may be relaxed to provide for 55 Itrs. per capita per day 
with a source within 0.5 km in the plains and 50 metres elevation in 
the hills after the coverage of a ll Not Covered and Partially Covered 
rural habitations in that State is achieved, as per the existing norms of 
40 litres per capita per day. This relaxation is subject to the condition that 
beneficiaries of the relaxed norms will share a part of the capital cost 
(which should not be less than 10%) and shoulder full responsibilities 
for subsequent Operation and Maintenance. 
(b) In case of schemes in quality affe cted villages or in multi-village 
schemes where the capital cost is very high, the schemes could be 
executed and implemented by the Government Departments/ 
Agencies/Board, and water is supplied to individual villages at 
157 

RAJYA SABHA [4 December, 2002] 
the periphery of each village. For drinking water distribution within the 
village, the beneficiaries would share a part of the capital cost (which 
should not be less than 10%) and shoulder full responsibilities for 
subsequent Operation and Maintenance of the village water distrbution 
network, while Government Department/ Board/Agency would maintian 
the main water supply system upto the village. 
Governments/Board/Agency may also charge water rates to the 
Panchayats/Village communities for bulk supply of water for drinking 
purpose. Such water charges and the village Operation and 
Maintenance cost would be fully met by the users/ beneficiaries. 
As per recent information available out of 50,379 rural habitations in 
Chhattisgarh all habitations have been fully covered and there are no Not 
Covered and Partially Covere d habitations in the State. This information is, 
however, provisional and subject to revision.

DR. MANMOHAN SINGH (Assam): Madam, I wish to draw your 
attention to a pamphlet which has been published by the Parliament

words have acquired a particular significance in the contemporary discussion 
of terrorism. So, I respectfully submit to you to instruct the Secretariat that 
this pamphlet, in its present form, should be withdrawn, and words like 
'terrorists' and 'extremists' should not be used for our leaders of freedom 
struggle, -particularly, the revolutionary leaders.

SHRI LALIT SURI: The last 12 years have witnessed the impact of 
liberalisation on the Indian economy. The process of liberalisation has 
redefined the role of the State and its relationship with business. Under an

changed the world over. The Government has never been the best of a 
business person. Bureaucrats are trained to be defensive, whereas businessmen 
are trained to be aggressive and competitive in the market. In areas in which 
the Government has had to compete with the private sector, where monopolies 
of the State have been dismantled, over  the price mechanism is not regulated 
by the State, the Government has not been able to survive competition with the 
private sector.. 
I have had some personal experience in the field of tourism and hotel 
industry. The failure of the Government in this area, in running hotels, is in 
sharp contrast to the privat e sector, which, in India, has been able to operate 
hotels considered to be amongst the best in the world. 
The basis philosophy behind disinvestment or privatisation is --where 
should the tax-payers' money be spent? Should the tax payers' money be 
invested in businesses in running hotels, in manufacturing steel, aluminium' 
and textiles, or, should it be used for the social sector to expand the base of 
education, health care, irrigation and other needs of the common man? The 
experience in these businesses has been that the Government taxes the people, 
invests his money in businesses, then loses this money. It then again taxes the 
people, draws out restructuring packages, most of which have not proved to be 
successful. In fact, it is the greatest in justice to a common man that his money 
is lost in business. In this context I quote an example of the U.K. experience 
where after disinvestment, merely the corporate tax realisation at the rate of 35 
per cent on profits brought in more money, than the total 100 per cent profits 
realised before disinvestment of these St ate enterprises. In addition, the U.K. 
Treasury made tens of billions of pounds from the sale of these companies and 
this money helped them to reduce taxes over many years, to make U.K. one of 
the lowest taxed countries in Europe. This also boosted consumer spending 
leading to higher growth and employment across the board in the economy. 
Even in our own country in the case of Modern Bread, Balco, CMC 
and others, there have been no job losses. On the other hand, higher 
production is leading to more employment directly and indirectly, higher taxes 
and other benefits to the economy. In fact, it is a win-win situation all the way.

DR. VIJAYA MALLYA (Karnataka): Hon. Madam Deputy 
Chairman, I thank you for this opportunity to speak. All my hon. colleagues 
have spoken with varying degrees of passion on the policy of disinvestment 
and, of course, the conduct of certain transaction relating to assets that have 
been divested. I am going to focus on disinvestment itself as a policy and 
share with this august House my view s. I am acutely aware of the time 
constraint and I shall be as brief as. I can. In my maiden speech, Madam, I 
raised the question of accountability in governan ce. Anything that the 
Government does should be as accountabl e to the elected representatives of 
the people, to the nominees of the Stat e and to the electorate themselves. I 
know that the Directive Principle of  our Constitution say that we are a 
democratic, socialist republic. . But does that mean that we are supposed to 
own manufacturing assets? The Govern ment should concentrate on areas 
where the private sector will not be interested. The 
268 

[4 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
private sector, typically the world over,  is interested in commerce. In a 
country like burs, where we have such a problem of lack of education, lack of 
adequate health facilities, poverty, I think, such sectors at affordable rates 
should be taken up by the Government and the business of running industries 
or manufacturing products should clearly be reserved for the private sector. In 
any case all the assets that we talk about, whether it is the Centaur Hotel or 
whether it is the IPCL, belong to all the taxpayers of this country. These 
assets must be put to work with a clear focus on return on investment. Merely 
saying that a particular public sector  undertaking is profitable is not a 
convincing argument because profita bility does not necessarily mean 
maximum efficiency. If we say that we  are efficient, then we must be 
competitive. We happen to have some sort of a phobia here in dealing with 
Government's intentions towards such public sector undertakings. The way to 
look at it would be to calculate the net return on investment to the 
Government. If the financial returns to the Government by privatisation, at 
whatever price, reflecting the preva iling circumstances produces a better 
return on investment as compared to the dividends that these companies pay, 
then they must be privatised. There has to be a focused economic approach 
rather than a political approach to the entire process of divestment. I would 
say that the Government should also re examine the price earning ratios of the 
public sector undertakings. My information that blue-chip public sector 
undertakings which were profitable, had a PE ratio between four and six 
times. Now these have actually risen after the divestment policy between 11 
and 85 times. This has increased the value of Government investment in the 
public sector units. If these have to be cashed out to provide a better return to 
the Government, then that is the correct policy to follow. We also have a 
phobia on monopolies and I do not understand why. There are some 
companies that have huge market shares. But equally like in the United States, 
you have the Anti-Trust laws. So, we can always protect the consumers' 
interests through regulation where exploitation is not possible. But just 
because a company is gigantic in size,  should not mean necessarily that we 
look differently at that company. It should, on the contrary, be appreciated 
that a company has achieved a world class size and economics of scale. 
Similarly, we have a phobia regarding the entry of multinationals. We seem to 
think that the sovereignty of India is threatened if large multinationals come 
and invest in our country. What is wrong if we today have several 
opportunities for IT professionals in the United States and why should we be 
worried about large companies coming into India either in the infrastructure 
269 

RAJYA SABHA [4 December, 2002] 
or petroleum or oil sector or for that matter in any business? We should 
welcome them and encourage competit ion because competition means that 
the consumers will benefit. And, there is no reason why the consumer should 
not benefit. There are too many rent seekers or, people, with vested interests, 
not only in the private sector but, we also know in the public sector as well, 
and these are the people who have their own vested interests to protect against 
privatisation or who make it a point to misrepresent the facts so that the 
privatisation policy can be criticised. It is fine to have a political debate and to 
protect political positions. But the reality of the situation is, that privatisation 
helps. In my State of Karnataka, we have invested Rs. 22,000 crores in public 
sector undertakings. One such ex ample is Mangalore Chemicals and 
Fertilizers Limited which was given to my group. Suffice it to say that we 
have implemented a Rs. 470-crore rehabilitation package and it is now a 
profit-making company. It is out of the BIFR. The Government of Karnataka 
could not run it. The MCF was on the verge of bankruptcy. And, today, we 
supply 85 per cent of the fertilizer ne eds of Karnataka State. This is one 
example of where a priv ate company can, actually, turn around what the 
public sector management had virtually run into the ground. 
Madam, the labour issue, arising ou t of privatisation, is not such a 
big issue. We have, in business, launched several Voluntary Retirement 
Schemes, which are designed to be nefit those who accept them. And, 
typically, if a private sector company takes over a public sector company -
once again, I refer to MCF -- yes; we offered a VRS. But, the remnant 
workmen, actually, were given a much better compensation package. So, to 
try to compare public sector  efficiency versus private sector efficiency is one 
thing. But to make huge capital out of it and say that divestment should not be 
pursued is something that is terribly retrograde. I may be referred to as a 
capitalist. But, nevertheless, I am an industrialist and I fully support 
privatisation and encourage the Government to use the proceeds of 
privatisation for tangible social benefits such as education and health care and 
there is really no need for the Government to be in the business of running 
industry.   Thank you.
